newsitem.title: FRANCE: Eurotunnel shareholders endorse debt restructuring.
newsitem.headline: Eurotunnel shareholders endorse debt restructuring.

text.p: Eurotunnel shareholders gave overwhelming support Thursday to a 70 billion franc ($11.7 billion) debt restructuring deal meant to put an end to the Anglo-French Channel Tunnel operator's crippling financial problems.

"The shareholders' vote was extraordinarily clear," Eurotunnel's French executive chairman, Patrick Ponsolle, said after the vote was announced to the packed shareholders' meeting. "We have turned a page for the company and I hope it is a happy page."
The debt deal will slash the shareholders' stake to 54.4 percent from 100 percent, with the rest going to Eurotunnel's banks in exchange for a reduction in its debt.
Ponsolle had warned shareholders that Eurotunnel faced bankruptcy if they rejected the plan.

Eurotunnel, unable to raise the revenues needed to repay the heavy debt borrowed to build the Channel Tunnel, had sought the restructuring to overcome the financial troubles which dogged it even before it began services in 1994.
It has been hobbled by a construction bill of 10 billion pounds ($16.9 billion), nearly twice the original estimate for the 31.6-mile link, and lower-than-targeted revenue since the service started.
The restructuring deal received 98 percent approval from British shareholders and between 96 percent and 97 percent approval from French shareholders attending the marathon six-hour meeting.

Eurotunnel needed the approval of holders of two-thirds of the French shares and three-quarters of the British shares at the meeting to pursue the deal struck with its leading bank lenders in April to restructure its debt mountain.
Ponsolle told the meeting Eurotunnel was on track for a better performance as long as shareholders approved the deal.

He forecast it would show a 2.72 billion franc ($461 million) loss this year, less than half the 1996 loss of 6.1 billion francs ($1.03 billion), and said he was "extremely confident" the group could turn a profit in 2005 and pay a dividend the following year.

Eurotunnel's interest payments will fall to 3.2 billion francs ($542.4 million) this year from 5.7 billion ($966 million) in 1996, giving it vital breathing space. The banks are giving up 22 billion francs ($3.7 billion) of interest payments over seven years.
Small shareholders, angry at the huge losses on their investment, had threatened to try to block the restructuring, saying it gave too much to the banks.
But prospects for its approval brightened last week after the French and British governments said they would consider extending Eurotunnel's operating license to 99 years from 65.
The governments also warned that if shareholders rejected the restructuring, they would be powerless to stop the banks from taking over Eurotunnel's operating license.
In the end, only Adacte, the most extreme of the three dissident investor groups, kept up its opposition to the plan.

A key question Thursday was whether Eurotunnel could muster a quorum of one-quarter of the total share capital to make the vote valid after a previous vote last month was cancelled when not enough shareholders attended.
Eurotunnel said 29.62 percent of the total votes that would have been eligible were represented this time.

The deal followed more than a year of negotiations with the banks. The steering group of Eurotunnel's 174 lenders has approved it in principle and now individual banks have to make a decision, but Eurotunnel Managing Director Georges-Christian Chazot was confident they would.
